report:
Conclusion: the claim is false as stated. Apples naturally make wax; washing removes some, so packers may add a thin food-grade coating to limit moisture loss and damage. FDA guidance treats waxed/coated produce as a regulated labeling/safety category, not a cancer hazard: https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/cpg-sec-562550-safety-and-labeling-waxed-coated-fruits-and-vegetables. Common coatings such as carnauba and shellac are described by the Northwest Horticultural Council as FDA-approved food coatings used safely for decades: https://nwhort.org/fruitcoatings/. EFSA lists carnauba wax (E903) as an authorized EU glazing agent and re-evaluated it as a food additive: https://www.efsa.europa.eu/el/efsajournal/pub/2880. A peer-reviewed review likewise notes commercial approved-wax coatings must meet food-additive regulations and are considered safe for consumption: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8535803/.

The cancer rumor likely confuses approved waxes with unrelated industrial waxes, pesticide residues, or morpholine emulsifiers/nitrosamine chemistry. Those are separate exposure/regulatory questions and do not show that normal food-grade apple wax causes cancer. Practical advice: rinse and rub apples under running water; buy organic if avoiding certain coatings matters to you. Evidence supports safety at typical intake, not carcinogenicity.
